To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) HCC in NA-FLD is an increasingly recognized entity, and its incidence seems to increase in developed countries, 2) HCCs in non-cir- rhotic fatty livers have been reported in a higher proportion in NAFLD, and 3) the genetic background of NAFLD patients seems to influence the risk of HCC, independently of the progression to cirrhosis.
the risk factors for HCC in NA-FLD include older age, severity of obesity, diabetes, and iron excess, but also the presence of specific genetic variants.
the role of environmental and inherited risk factors is magnified in nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) related HCC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the molecular mechanisms involved in hepatocarcinogenesis, with a particular focus on nonalcoholic fatty-liver disease.
the role of genetic and environmental factors on the development of liver disease, including nonalcoholic fatty disease and its complications, such as liver fibrosis and hepatocellular carcinoma.
the identification and characterization of novel risk factors for HCC in NAFFLD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
NAFLD is a strong risk factor for the development of HCC, and that it is a condition in which genetic and environmental factors are both important in the carcinogenesis process.
NAFLD is a common condition that may predispose to HCV and HBV related HCC and to a lesser extent to HCC not related to viral infection.
the risk factors of HCC in NAFA are the same as those of cirrhosis, with the addition of the I148M PNPLA3 variant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
NAFLD is a major risk factor for HCC and that its progression is influenced by genetic and environmental determinants.

NAFLD-associated HCCs are a distinct entity, which is more frequent in non-cirrhosis and in the young, and which is associated with a higher risk of cancer-related mortality, especially in patients with diabetes and obesity.
the genetic background is an important determinant of HCC development in NAFLD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
NAFLD is an emerging risk factor for HCC, and that the identification of genetic factors predisposing to cancer may help to stratify patients at high risk and to develop new preventive strategies.
the genetic and environmental determinants of HCC in NAFFLD are still largely unexplored, but their identification may provide new opportunities to prevent and treat the disease.
HCC risk assessment in NAFLD should be individualized and based on a combination of genetic, clinical and histological factors.
